props.title: All About Eve
props.initialSlug: Ambitious understudy plots to steal actress's stardom

sections.content: All About Eve revolutionized Hollywood's portrayal of female ambition and rivalry. Bette Davis delivers a career-defining performance as Margo Channing, an aging Broadway star gradually being usurped by the seemingly innocent Eve Harrington (Anne Baxter). Joseph L. Mankiewicz's razor-sharp screenplay creates a fascinating study of theater world politics and the price of fame. The film's influence echoes through later works like Showgirls (1995) and Black Swan (2010), though none match its sophisticated blend of wit and psychological warfare.

sections.content: The film's examination of aging in entertainment remains painfully relevant. Like Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962) and Mulholland Drive (2001), it explores how Hollywood discards women as they age. Mankiewicz's direction creates an atmosphere of mounting dread beneath the glamorous surface, while George Sanders' acidic theater critic Addison DeWitt provides commentary that cuts to the bone. The film's 14 Academy Award nominations (a record at the time) reflect its technical and artistic mastery.

The backstage drama genre gained new sophistication with All About Eve. While earlier films like Stage Door (1937) touched on theatrical ambition, none had dared show such calculated manipulation. The film's DNA appears in modern works like Opening Night (1977) and Birdman (2014), which similarly blur the lines between performance and reality. Its exploration of identity theft and social climbing predates similar themes in Single White Female (1992) and The Talented Mr. Ripley (1999). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: The film's impact on depicting female relationships in cinema cannot be overstated. Later works like The Devils Wears Prada (2006) and Clouds of Atlas (2012) echo its examination of mentorship turned toxic. Mankiewicz's technique of using multiple narrators and flashbacks influenced films like Rashomon (1950) and Citizen Kane (1941), showing how subjective truth can be in the entertainment world.
